title: HTM: A Hybrid Classical-Quantum Computation Model
authors: Guoqiang Shu, Zongjiang Yi, Jinyang Yao, Haomiao Dong, Zhihang Li, Fudong Liu, Zheng Shan
abstract: Classical and quantum computers have achieved collaborative computation and completed applications across numerous fields. Nevertheless, the absence of a unified hybrid computation model has led to issues such as non-standardized engineering architecture design, ambiguous task partitioning criteria and so on. To address these issues, this research proposes a hybrid classical-quantum computation model (HTM). By constructing unified state sets and transition function representations, HTM clarifies hybrid control logic and implements a control-sharing mechanism. Simultaneously, a comprehensive complexity calculation method based on entanglement and superposition was proposed, supporting computation task partitioning and resource scheduling. The HTM fills a theoretical gap in the classical-quantum hybrid computation area and implements the joint promotion and development of computing models and hardware.
summary: This paper introduces the Hybrid Classical-Quantum Computation Model (HTM) to solve the architectural inconsistencies in current hybrid computing approaches. By unifying state sets and transition functions, HTM provides a rigorous theoretical foundation for scheduling and controlling joint classical-quantum tasks. This standardization is vital for advancing the engineering and development of practical quantum hardware.
main_problem: The lack of a unified theoretical model for hybrid classical-quantum computation leads to non-standardized architectures and ambiguous resource partitioning criteria.
main_result: The proposed Hybrid Classical-Quantum Computation Model (HTM) provides a standardized framework that unifies state representation and control logic for classical and quantum processes.
method: The model defines the HTM using a unified state set and transition function, supported by a comprehensive complexity calculation method based on entanglement and superposition.
model_or_system: The HTM is a theoretical computational model featuring a classical track and a quantum track on a shared tape, controlled by a unified controller that manages synchronization and resource sharing.
key_observables: Time complexity (path length/number of gates) and Space complexity (number of state records/tape cells accessed).
important_parameters: The number of qubits ($n$), the size of the entanglement measure ($|E|$), and the number of iterations ($K$).
main_assumptions: The model adopts deterministic state transitions, and classical states are treated as a special, pure case of quantum states.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the Hybrid Turing Machine Architecture, showing the unified control managing dual read/write heads for classical and quantum operations.
paper_structure: The paper first identifies the gap in hybrid computation models, then formally proposes the HTM structure (7-tuple definition), details the control-sharing mechanism, and finally analyzes the resulting polynomial time complexity compared to exponential classical simulation.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, formal framework for integrating classical control flow with quantum unitary evolution, which is crucial for designing next-generation quantum hardware architectures.
